title: Power Armor
subtitle: What the Armor Leaves Behind · Chapter 9 of 40
content:
Power armor training began because I made one arrogant remark.

This was my fault.

Danse had been repairing a Brotherhood frame in the garage when I said, “It can’t be that difficult. You climb in and walk.”

He slowly lowered the wrench.

Haylen, sitting three feet away, looked delighted.

Rhys whispered, “Oh, no.”

Danse turned toward me.

“Climb in.”

I should have recognized the trap.

Instead I said, “Gladly.”

Ten minutes later I was trapped inside several hundred pounds of technology trying not to walk through a wall.

“Small movements,” Danse called from outside.

“I am making small movements.”

“You just kicked a toolbox across the garage.”

“It was in my operational area.”

“It was six feet away.”

“Was.”

Haylen covered her mouth.

"Don't laugh," I said from inside the frame.

"I'm not." Haylen's shoulders made a convincing argument against her.

Danse pointed at the orange lever beside my right hip. "Emergency release. Tell me what it does."

"Gets me out when I've embarrassed myself enough?"

"It disengages the rear locking assembly." His expression didn't change. "If the hydraulics lose power, you need to know how to exit without waiting for an external operator. Show me."

I reached for it. Nothing happened.

"Wrong lever," Haylen said, suddenly serious. She came over and held her finger beside a faded caution stripe. "This is the one you can reach while the frame is powered down. The orange one only releases the exterior latch."

Danse leaned in to inspect the marking. Somebody had applied a fresh coat of paint over most of the old label.

"Who signed off on that?" he asked.

Rhys stopped smiling. "I did the exterior, sir. Wasn't told the safety label was underneath."

"Then we correct it. And check the others before anyone else trains."

Haylen fetched a marker and documented the latch position while Danse walked me through the actual release. I wasn't allowed to repeat the drill until I could find it without looking.

When I finally climbed free, my knees felt like jelly. Danse offered a hand; I took it, braced for another lecture, and got something more useful.

"Good correction," he said. "You asked when the instructions didn't match the machine."

"I didn't ask. I complained."

"In your case the distinction is not always apparent." His mouth moved a fraction. I laughed so hard I had to sit on the garage step.

Danse did not laugh.

That would have been less humiliating.

He watched me with the solemn focus of a man observing a controlled demolition.

“Again. Shift your weight before the step.”

“I know how walking works.”

“Not in armor, apparently.”

I turned too quickly.

The frame lurched.

Danse caught the chest plate with both hands.

“Stop.”

I froze.

He was close enough that I could see his face through the open frame.

“Don’t fight the servos,” he said. “The suit amplifies what you give it. If you panic and overcorrect, it overcorrects with you.”

“Easy for you to say.”

“I fell the first time.”

I stared.

He stared back.

“Paladin Danse fell over in power armor?”

“Once.”

“Tell me everything.”

“No.”

“Did anyone see?”

“No.”

“Was Cutler there?”

His expression changed.

For a second I regretted asking.

Then he exhaled through his nose.

“Yes.”

“And?”

“He never stopped mentioning it.”

I smiled.

“Then I respect him more already.”

Danse’s eyes softened.

“He would have liked you.”

The words slipped out.

Neither of us moved.

I felt the power armor’s motors humming around me.

“Yeah?” I asked.

“Yes.”

His hands were still braced against the frame near my ribs.

Not touching me.

Close enough that my body noticed anyway.

Danse seemed to realize the same thing.

He stepped back.

“Try again.”

His voice was rougher.

I obeyed.

Once I stopped trying to control the suit like a stubborn brahmin, it became easier. The weight shifted where I wanted. Hydraulic strength turned steps into certainty. The world felt smaller from inside all that metal.

“I understand the appeal,” I admitted.

Danse folded his arms.

“Of course you do.”

“It’s like being a building that can punch people.”

“That is an appalling description.”

“Accurate, though.”

“No.”

“Can I keep it?”

“Absolutely not.”

By midday he had me walking, turning, crouching, and stepping over obstacles without destroying station property.

The final lesson was emergency exit.

Danse opened the frame and showed me how to release the locks manually.

“If the power core fails, don’t stay inside.”

“Seems obvious.”

“It isn’t when people think the armor is safer than whatever’s outside.”

His hands moved over the latches with practiced speed.

“Armor is equipment. Not security.”

Something about the sentence caught me.

I looked at him.

Danse was focused on the mechanism.

“You believe that?”

“What?”

“That armor isn’t security.”

He glanced up.

“It’s steel.”

“You wear it whenever possible.”

“It’s practical.”

“You also wear the invisible kind.”

The garage went quiet.

Haylen had wisely disappeared sometime in the last hour.

Danse’s expression closed.

“I don’t know what you mean.”

“Yes, you do.”

He stepped away from the frame.

“This isn’t the time.”

“Fine.”

I did not push.

That was something I was learning with him too: pressure was not the same as persistence. Some doors opened if I waited near them without pretending they were not doors.

I climbed out of the armor.

My knees felt strangely light after carrying the suit’s weight.

Danse handed me a bottle of water.

“Hydrate.”

“Yes, sir.”

“I’m serious.”

“So am I.”

He frowned while I drank.

A drop ran down my chin. I wiped it away.

His eyes followed the movement.

Then snapped back to my face.

Interesting.

I lowered the bottle.

Danse suddenly found the armor frame extremely compelling.

“Your footwork improved.”

“Thank you.”

“You still turn too sharply.”

“There’s the corrective feedback.”

“It’s necessary.”

“I was worried you were ill.”

He reached for the wrench.

I caught his wrist.

The gesture was impulsive.

Danse stopped.

His skin was warm.

So was mine, abruptly.

I released him.

“Sorry.”

“No.”

He looked at the place where my hand had been.

“It’s fine.”

The silence stretched.

Outside, a vertibird did not appear. No alarm sounded. Rhys did not walk in to rescue either of us from ourselves.

Danse cleared his throat.

“You did well today.”

“Just well?”

His eyes met mine.

“Outstanding.”

There was no sarcasm in it.

I smiled before I could stop myself.

He looked away first.

That evening, I found a set of handwritten power armor maintenance notes beside my bedroll.

The handwriting was blocky, precise, and unmistakably Danse’s.

At the bottom he had added one line:

DO NOT KICK TOOLBOXES.

I laughed loudly enough to wake Rhys.

From the other side of the station, Danse pretended not to hear.

The training did not end with walking.

Danse believed that if I was going to use Brotherhood equipment even temporarily, I was going to learn every way it could kill me before an enemy got the chance.

“Fusion core failure.”

“Exit the frame.”

“Hydraulic lock in the right leg.”

“Shift weight, disengage assist, call you something unprintable.”

“The third step is not part of procedure.”

“It improves morale.”

He made me repeat emergency egress until I could do it with my eyes closed.

Literally.

I stood inside the frame with the helmet display dark while Danse circled me.

“Left release.”

I found it by touch.

“Manual torso latch.”

Found that too.

“Rear access.”

I reached back, caught the handle, and pulled.

Nothing happened.

I pulled harder.

Still nothing.

Danse swore.

“What?”

“Don’t move.”

“That phrase is never comforting.”

He stepped behind me and worked at the jammed latch. His chest brushed the rear armor plate as he leaned around the frame. One hand closed over mine to reposition my grip.

“Here.”

His voice was suddenly much closer without a helmet between us.

I became aware of several completely irrelevant facts at once: the heat of his hand, the rasp of stubble when he spoke near my ear, the way he smelled like gun oil and clean sweat.

The latch released with a metallic crack.

I nearly fell backward into him.

Danse caught my waist.

Neither of us moved.

“Oh,” I said.

“Yes.”

His hands remained exactly where they had landed.

I turned my head.

He was looking at me with the expression of a man who had just discovered an unexploded mine under his own boot.

“You can let go.”

“I’m aware.”

He did not.

A second passed.

Then another.

From the station doorway Haylen yelled, “Paladin, Rhys wants to know if you’re planning to train the recruit or marry the power armor.”

Danse released me so fast I almost fell for real.

“I am not a recruit!” I shouted back.

“Noted!”

Danse walked three full steps away and stared at the wall.

I climbed out of the frame.

“Are you all right?” I asked with criminal innocence.

“Yes.”

“You look warm.”

“It’s the ambient temperature.”

“It’s forty-eight degrees.”

“The training room retains heat.”

“There’s a hole in the roof.”

He turned.

“Do you want to complete the lesson or not?”

I bit the inside of my cheek.

“Yes, Paladin.”

“Good.”

He took a breath.

“Again.”

We practiced until my muscles shook.

When I finally climbed out for the last time, he handed me water and leaned against the armor rack beside me.

“You did well.”

“Even with the toolbox?”

“Especially after the toolbox. You corrected the mistake.”

I looked at him over the bottle.

“You always do that.”

“Do what?”

“Treat mistakes like they’re only useful if you learn from them.”

“That’s generally true.”

“Even yours?”

His face changed.

The question had gone somewhere I had not meant it to.

“Yes,” he said after a moment. “Especially mine.”

I thought of four names on a wall.

Danse looked away.

Then, quieter, “Though some lessons cost more than they should.”

The frame hissed softly behind me as its servos cooled.

Danse picked up the toolbox I had kicked earlier and began returning everything to its assigned slot. I watched him line up three wrenches by size.

“You know,” I said, “normal people would leave that until later.”

“Normal people lose tools.”

“Normal people also occasionally enjoy themselves.”

He slid the smallest wrench into place. “Training can be enjoyable.”

“You enjoyed watching me nearly walk through a wall.”

His mouth betrayed him.

“I did not.”

“You absolutely did.”

“Your recovery was impressive.”

“That is a confession with extra steps.”

Danse shook his head, but the tension around his eyes eased. The lesson about mistakes was not abstract for him. He treated every error like something that had to justify its cost. Maybe that was why watching me make a harmless one unsettled him and amused him at the same time.

Some mistakes only cost a toolbox.

I wanted him to learn that too.

I did not reach for him.

Not yet.

Instead I set the water down and climbed back into the frame.

“Again?”

His eyes returned to me.

This time the smile came openly.

“Again.”
